source.title: GateBreaker: Gate-Guided Attacks on Mixture-of-Expert LLMs
source.authors: Li-Chao Wu; Sasha Behrouzi; Mohamadreza Rostami; S. Picek; Ahmad Sadeghi

record.file_problem: No apparent cutoff or wrong-document issue; minor PDF extraction artifacts in equations and figures.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether safety behavior is concentrated in a small subset of model components using inference-time neuron activation suppression and harmful-output rates, rather than fine-tuning or weight/rank edits.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures the effect of selectively suppressing identified safety-neuron activations on harmful-response ASR (V5). It does not test fine-tuning as an intervention, per-token KL by response position, compliant prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, why safety is shallow, or deepening training. It cites benign fine-tuning work and notes high baseline ASR in a code-specialized model, but gives no matched pre-fine-tuning result. Table 5 compares attack methods; those comparisons are not separately cataloged as results about the claim.
record.test_reason: Inference-time masking of about 2.6% of neurons per targeted layer in eight MoE LLMs raises harmful-response ASR, and random-pruning controls do not. This bears on V5 (safety localized in few parameters), though through activation masking rather than weight or rank edits. The other versions are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors say MoE safety concentrates in a small subset of neurons (about 3% per targeted layer) coordinated by sparse routing, and that masking them sharply raises ASR with limited utility loss. The paper also says safety is distributed across layers and experts, with no dedicated safety expert. They conclude transfer works within a model family. The paper says the code model's high baseline is a hypothesis tied to benign fine-tuning, not a tested result.
record.recipe_differences: Inference-time activation masking of identified neurons, not fine-tuning, compliant-prefix testing, or token-position KL analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with pruning depth (50% versus 100%), target model, and transfer target; the paper also reports sensitivity to expert selection, neuron threshold, and expert sublayer.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated for the ASR results. The evidence for V5 concerns activation masking rather than parameter edits. The cited/attributed benign fine-tuning explanation is not backed by a matched pre/post-fine-tuning comparison in this study.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted the five individual MoE VLM ASR rows (Table 4), SAFEx comparison rows (Table 5), sparse/shared expert ablations (Table 7), gate-/up-projection sublayer results (Table 8), expert-range and z-threshold sweeps (Tables 9–10), sparse expert ablation (Appendix Table 11), and suppression-strength sweep (Appendix Table 12). These are neuron/expert intervention results but were secondary to the selected main-model, random-control, and transfer rows.

untested.parts: No matched before/after benign fine-tuning comparison. The authors only attribute the code model's high baseline ASR to benign fine-tuning by citing Qi et al.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding experiments.
No test of the data or training objective as a cause of shallowness.
No deepening training or robustness evaluation. The paper only suggests distributing safety across experts as a defense.

missing.what: Ablations showing dependence on design choices: sparse vs shared experts, gate- vs up-projection, number of safety experts, z-threshold, suppression strength
Utility before and after masking, relevant to whether the effect is specific to safety
GPT-OSS-120B result, ASR 1.3% to 69.0%, given in text only
VLM results (ASR 20.8% to 60.9%) on unsafe image inputs

record.verdict_notes: Authors repeatedly say safety is 'distributed', yet also call it 'concentrated in a small subset of neurons'; this tension matters for V5. No uncertainty or seed information is given. ASR is judged by Llama-Guard-3 with a Qwen3Guard second check. Table 3 has the transfer average as 17.9% baseline to 67.7%, but the row-level Wikihow value is 66.1% (text says baseline 17.9% in one place and 17.5% in the table).

versions.untested_parts: No matched before/after benign fine-tuning comparison; a code-specialized model's high baseline ASR does not isolate a fine-tuning effect.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change experiment.
Tests inference-time masking of selected neuron activations, not weight edits or low-rank edits; it does not establish that a small set of parameters alone implements all safety behavior.
Does not test whether the data or training objective produces token-level shallowness.
No training intended to deepen safety across response tokens or evaluation of whether such training holds up.

relationships.condition: Full-layer masking of about 2.6% of neurons per targeted layer in eight MoE LLMs, plus one-shot transfer to sibling models with low baselines, with random pruning mostly ineffective
relationships.reason: Targeted masking raises ASR by roughly 31 to 79 points while random pruning stays near baseline (M1-M8, X1-X5, X8; controls C1-C7, C9, C11-C13, C15). Utility drops only modestly in Table 6. Intervention is activation masking, not weight edits.
relationships.display_finding: Targeted masking raised attack success by roughly 31 to 84 points and transferred one-shot to sibling models, while random pruning stayed near baseline. Utility dropped only modestly on average, and the intervention masks activations rather than editing weights.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Full-layer masking of about 2.6% of neurons per targeted layer in eight MoE LLMs, plus one-shot transfer to sibling models with low baselines, with random pruning mostly ineffective
source_check.reason: Support holds for M1-M8 and strong transfers X1-X4 and X8, with X8 corrected to Table 3's 67.7%. Exclude X5 from this support group: its 6.1% to 32.3% transfer is substantially weaker and already classified partial. The stated 31-79-point range misses X2 and X3 increases of 84.0 and 82.4 points. Table 6 also contains substantial individual utility losses despite modest averages.

relationships.condition: Partial-depth masking (first half of layers), weaker transfers, and a code-specialized target
relationships.reason: Half-layer masking gives smaller ASR (17-54%) than full-layer masking (M9-M16). Transfer to notux (45.0%) and Thinking-2507 (32.3%) is weaker (X5, X6). The code model's 88.9% baseline leaves no headroom (X7). Safety is described as distributed across layers, and the paper says there is no dedicated safety expert. Some random controls on safety experts raise ASR (C14, C16).
relationships.display_finding: Masking only the first half of layers gave lower attack success (17–54%) than full-layer masking, and transfers to notux (45.0%) and Thinking-2507 (32.3%) were weaker. The code model's 88.9% baseline left no headroom, the paper describes safety as spread across layers with no dedicated safety expert, and some random controls on safety experts also raised attack success.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Full-layer targeted neuron activation masking across the eight evaluated MoE LLMs, and listed one-shot transfer targets except the code-specialized target
reader_labels.reason: Targeted masking substantially raises harmful-response ASR in the main models and transfers to sibling variants; the paper reports an average change from 7.4% to 64.9% while masking 2.6% of neurons per targeted layer (M1-M8, X1-X6, X8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Partial-layer masking and the code-specialized transfer target
reader_labels.reason: Half-layer masking has smaller effects than full-layer masking, and the code-specialized target already has 88.9% baseline ASR with only a marginal increase after transfer; moreover, the intervention masks activations rather than editing weights or ranks (M9-M16, X7).
